run.question: We're getting mapping errors and slow indexing on our events index. Can you check the field mappings for our app-188-index-* indexes and tell me if any have an unusually high number of fields? What's the exact field count for each?

report.summary: Field mappings were read for all four indices matching app-188-index-* (app-188-index-a, -b, -c and -x). Field counts are: app-188-index-a = 10, app-188-index-b = 10, app-188-index-c = 10, app-188-index-x = 523 top-level fields — 655 mapped fields when the 132 'keyword' multi-fields are included. app-188-index-x is therefore the outlier at roughly 52x (top-level) to 65x (including multi-fields) the field count of its siblings; its extra fields are 130 each of numbered counter_*, flag_*, label_* and metric_* fields plus event and user_id. This is an observed mapping-bloat finding, and the numbered-field pattern is consistent with dynamic mapping of a document carrying 520 generated field names (hypothesis, since the mappings do not show how or when the fields were created). The reported 'mapping errors' and 'slow indexing' could not be verified: the only index stats available show app-188-index-x with index_total=2, index_failed=0, index_time_in_millis=4, and the cluster holds only these four indices, so there are no Elasticsearch/server log indices in this target to search for mapper_parsing_exception or 'Limit of total fields' messages, and index settings (e.g. index.mapping.total_fields.limit) are not readable with the available tools. No latency baseline exists, so no trend is claimed.

claims.text: The pattern app-188-index-* matches exactly four indices: app-188-index-a, app-188-index-b, app-188-index-c (each 0 documents, 227b store) and app-188-index-x (1 document). A separate wildcard listing of all indices returned the same four indices and nothing else, so the cluster holds no other index (for example no log or metrics index) in this target.
Top-level mapped property count per index: app-188-index-a = 10, app-188-index-b = 10, app-188-index-c = 10, app-188-index-x = 523.

app-188-index-x has no nested object properties but 132 of its top-level fields carry multi-fields, and those multi-fields total exactly 132 subfields (one each, named 'keyword' on sampled entries such as event_type and label_0003), giving 655 mapped fields in total vs 523 top-level names.

The 523 fields of app-188-index-x follow a generated pattern: 1 @timestamp field, 1 event field, 1 user_id field, and 130 fields in each of the prefixes counter_, flag_, label_ and metric_ (e.g. counter_0001, counter_0005, counter_0009 ... metric_0516), with numbered suffixes stepping by 4.

Type distribution of the 523 top-level fields in app-188-index-x: 132 text, 131 long, 130 boolean, 129 float and 1 date. The mapping does not record 'dynamic', 'date_detection' or 'numeric_detection' settings (these returned null).

app-188-index-a, -b and -c share one identical, small schema of 10 top-level fields: @timestamp (date), action (keyword), duration_ms (integer), error_message (text), event_type (keyword), ip_address (ip), metadata (object with no mapped sub-properties), session_id (keyword), status (keyword), user_id (keyword); none of them has any multi-field.

Cumulative index statistics at query time: app-188-index-x has index_total=2, index_failed=0, index_time_in_millis=4, docs.count=1, docs.deleted=1, total_size_in_bytes=209030 (store 209403b); app-188-index-a has index_total=0 and no documents. These counters are cumulative since index creation, not windowed values.

The 520 numbered counter_/flag_/label_/metric_ fields in app-188-index-x most likely came from dynamic mapping of document field names generated per event or per payload position, rather than from a deliberate explicit mapping; the mappings alone do not show which mechanism created them or when.

The 523/655-field mapping of app-188-index-x is a plausible contributor to slow indexing on that index (larger cluster-state updates and per-document field handling), but no indexing-latency baseline or windowed indexing metric was observed, so it is not confirmed as the cause of the reported slowness.

If mapping errors are occurring on writes into app-188-index-*, the most likely shape is mapper_parsing_exception or a total-fields limit rejection on app-188-index-x, whose 655 mapped fields are the only ones large enough to approach a field cap; this is unverified because index.mapping.total_fields.limit was not readable and no Elasticsearch error log index exists in this target.

No index-level failure is recorded in the available statistics: app-188-index-x reports index_failed=0 and index_failed_due_to_version_conflict=0, and complete index_time_in_millis of 4 for 2 indexing operations; this does not cover rejected bulk items and cannot confirm or rule out mapper_parsing_exception.

The field bloat is localized: app-188-index-a, -b and -c each still map exactly 10 top-level fields with no multi-fields and no metadata sub-properties, so the high field count is not a property of the whole app-188-index-* family.

Retrieve index.mapping.total_fields.limit (and any index template or dynamic template applied to app-188-index-*) for app-188-index-x via the Elasticsearch settings API, since the available mapping tooling does not expose settings.

For the numbered-field family in app-188-index-x, consider mapping the generated field group as a single flattened or disabled field (or enforcing a template with dynamic: strict for counter_/flag_/label_/metric_ prefixes) so the field count stops growing, and then reindex/rollover once the target mapping is fixed.

gaps: Mapping error messages could not be read: the target holds only the four app-188-index-* indices (no logstash/filebeat or Elasticsearch server log index), and no tool exposes Elasticsearch server logs; the change_history integration is listed as not_integrated.
Index settings, including index.mapping.total_fields.limit, are not exposed by the available mapping tools, so whether app-188-index-x is at or near a field cap is unknown.

Whether the 520 numbered fields were created dynamically or declared explicitly, and when they were created, cannot be determined: mappings carry no timestamps and all views describe only the moment of the query, not the incident window.
Slow indexing is unverified: no windowed indexing-latency metric or baseline was available; only cumulative counters (index_total=2, index_time_in_millis=4 for app-188-index-x) were observed.
Field counts are what the mappings returned at query time; the number of fields actually present in documents was not measured, and a single document was observed in app-188-index-x only.

Errors from bulk-item rejections (for example mapper_parsing_exception per document) are not reflected in index_failed counters, so their absence in the statistics is not evidence that no mapping errors occurred.
next_steps: Read app-188-index-x settings (index.mapping.total_fields.limit, dynamic setting, applied templates) from the Elasticsearch API or Kibana index management.
Search Elasticsearch server or shipping-pipeline logs for 'mapper_parsing_exception' and 'Limit of total fields' around the period when indexing was slow.
Obtain an indexing-latency baseline (for example index_time_in_millis delta per interval and bulk rejection counts) before and during the slow period to compare against.
Inspect the single document in app-188-index-x to confirm whether it carries all 520 numbered field names, which would establish the dynamic-mapping mechanism.
